item.title: The Science Talk Signs the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
item.description:
We signed the European Commission’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, under Section 2, as a deployer of generative AI systems. That puts The Science Talk in the same signatory pool as Bulgari, Getty Images, Lenovo, and Lufthansa. Section 1 of the framework counts Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Mistral among its signatories.

Why this, why now

The AI Act’s transparency obligations become legally binding on 2 August 2026. These are the rules that require AI-generated and AI-modified content to be marked and disclosed. It gives signatories “a streamlined, predictable and legally certain pathway,” regardless of which national authority ends up supervising them.

item.title: Regulation as a Feature: The Case for AI Transparency
item.description:
Every conversation about the EU AI Act’s transparency rules starts from the same assumption: this is a cost to minimize. Add the disclosure, tick the box, move on. This framing gets the opportunity backwards. AI transparency, done properly, is a genuine competitive advantage for a small AI-using team that competes against operators who treat it as an afterthought.

The obligation, stated plainly

Article 50 of the AI Act requires providers of certain AI systems to state clearly that people interact with AI. It also requires marking of AI-generated or manipulated content, including deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. These duties apply from 2 August 2026. Following the 2026 Digital Omnibus, generative AI systems already on the market before that date get an extended transitional period to 2 December 2026 to comply with the content-marking requirement specifically.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 5: AI Practices You're Banned From Using

item.title: Recommender Systems: Even EU Regulators Don't Agree Which Law Applies
item.description:

The European Commission’s own review of the Digital Services Act names recommender systems as one of the most-cited areas of stakeholder ambiguity. The review does not dispute the confusion. It documents it.

You may build or operate a recommender system in the EU. It could be a “you might also like” feature, a personalized feed, or a ranking algorithm. This admission from the regulator matters more than any single law firm’s reading of the rules.

item.title: Claude Usage Limits 2026: The Complete Guide
item.description:
Claude’s usage limits are one of the most-asked, least-clearly-answered questions for daily work use. Help articles, forum threads, and blog posts scatter the mechanics, plan differences, and cost tradeoffs. This guide puts the complete picture in one place: mechanics, plans, cost, and a decision framework.

How Claude’s usage limits actually work

Claude’s usage limit is not a daily message cap. It does not reset at midnight. It runs on a rolling 5-hour window that starts from the moment you send your first message. If you send your first message at 09:47, your window runs until 14:47. It does not run to the top of the next hour or to a fixed daily timestamp.

item.title: The AI Act Omnibus Delay: Relief or a Trap for Small Teams?
item.description: The headline version of the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI is simple. The EU pushed the high-risk rules back. Stand-alone high-risk systems now have until 2 December 2027. High-risk systems embedded in regulated products have until 2 August 2028. Both dates are later than the original 2 August 2026 date. This headline will cost some small teams a compliance scramble in eighteen months. They will read “delayed” as “cancelled” and stop preparing.

item.title: GPAI Code of Practice: Provider vs. Deployer, Explained
item.description: Does the GPAI Code of Practice apply to you? For most teams that build AI-powered products, the answer is no. The Code is the European Commission’s voluntary compliance tool for providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act. The Commission published it on 10 July 2025 after input from more than 1,000 stakeholders. It binds model providers, not the teams that build on top of their models. This guide walks through the provider-vs-deployer test, what each of the Code’s three chapters covers, and what a downstream team building on GPT, Claude, or similar models should take from it.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 25: When You Become the AI 'Provider'
item.description:
Most agencies I speak to treat the EU AI Act as someone else’s problem. They use AI tools, so they assume the heavy obligations sit upstream with OpenAI, Anthropic, or whichever vendor built the model. Almost none of them have read Article 25. This clause moves the provider’s entire obligation set onto ordinary businesses through work they do every week.

This is the most overlooked liability transfer in the Act for creative, marketing, consulting, and research agencies. It does not require you to build a model. It requires you to put a logo on something, adjust it, or point it at a new job. These are the exact activities agencies are paid for.

Difference between Communication and Dissemination

Communication and dissemination aren’t the same thing — and treating them separately is what makes your research stand out.

Communication builds your credibility over time. It’s broad and ongoing — papers, conference talks, the general visibility you build just by doing good research and showing up in your field.

Dissemination works differently. It’s the deliberate, targeted transfer of your research to specific audiences who can use it — think podcasts, videos, webinars, press releases.

item.title: EU CADA Sovereignty Tiers: What the Four Cloud Levels Mean
item.description:
Key takeaways

  • CADA introduces four cloud sovereignty assurance levels for EU public procurement. Four measurable criteria define each level.
  • Member States and EU entities must do a sovereignty risk assessment for every cloud use case. This is mandatory.
  • The compliance requirement cascades. Organisations that supply public bodies will face the same questions indirectly.
  • The four criteria are specific enough to start an internal mapping exercise now, before the EU publishes formal guidance.

The EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) was proposed on 3 June 2026. It introduces four cloud sovereignty tiers for public sector procurement. A specific set of criteria defines each tier, and a mandatory risk assessment process attaches to each one. This is the first time the EU has built a formal sovereignty classification system directly into procurement law. Most European organisations buy cloud services from non-EU providers. If your organisation buys cloud from any provider, the tier you sit in will soon become a procurement compliance question, not a strategic preference.

item.title: AI Vendor Lock-In: The Startup Audit You Should Run Before Scale

What stopped me from reading it as a policy document was not the numbers. It was the mechanism. The four vectors of AI vendor lock-in it describes at EU scale, proprietary formats, API dependencies, long contracts, and network effects, are the same ones startups build into their products right now, sprint by sprint.

item.description: The European Parliament’s December 2025 study on software and cyber dependencies puts a number on something most enterprise leaders already sense but have not yet formally mapped. item.title: Claude Adoption in European Research: The Infrastructure Gap
item.description: I have watched the conversation about Claude in European research circles for some time now. The discussion almost always centers on product quality. SciArt of the month - Feb 2023

This science art piece shows cell nuclei that contain DNA in the eye of a developing zebrafish. The nuclei were stained using DAPI staining that binds to the DNA, imaged with a state-of-the-art AiryScan microscope, and the images were subsequently processed. Using biomedical image analysis to extract, separate, and depth-code these data, we can start to see nuclei closer to the viewer in black, and those further away using an image gradient like red-green-blue-cyan-magenta and finally the yellow, which is furthest in the tissue. These data help us understand how the eye is formed. Check out more here: https://twitter.com/Zeeks_Art
